hardDay.heading: Hard day? Start here.
hardDay.body:
If you can't take a step this week, that's okay. Your assignment this week is honesty and one trusted believer. That's it. Not performance.

Tell God the truth in one plain sentence. Then tell one person who loves Jesus and loves you. Ask them to pray with you.

When you have the strength, read Chapter 8, the section "A Pastoral Word to the Sincerely Stuck." It was written for days like this one.

If you are in danger, or you are having thoughts of not wanting to live, please stop here and reach out now. In the U.S., call or text 988, or call 911. Then tell a pastor or a trusted believer today.

bookRef.section: A Pastoral Word to the Sincerely Stuck

read.heading: Read first: the Introduction
read.body:
Before we do anything in this app, open the book. Read the Introduction, "The Great Christian Standstill." It's short. Read the whole thing, then come back.

Here's why I send you there first. This app asks the questions. The book does the teaching. If you skip the reading, the questions won't land, and you'll end up with one more thing on your phone that feels like motion but isn't.

As you read, watch for two things. First, the holy-sounding sentences we reach for when we're stuck, the ones about trusting, waiting, and doors God will open. Sometimes those sentences are true. Sometimes they're a covering. Second, watch for the chair. I tell you how I was taught to trust God like a chair, and how my picture of trust stopped at sitting while the gifts God gave me sat unused.

If you've ever called a freeze "faith," you're in the right place. Read with a pen. Mark the line that sounds like you. Then tap the button below and we'll take it one honest step at a time.
read.quote: we baptize that freeze with holy language.
prompts: Which line in the Introduction sounded most like you?

pulse.heading: The pulse: faith rests, and faith moves
pulse.body:
Here's the heart of the Introduction in plain words. You don't have to choose between trusting God and living on purpose. Scripture holds both. God works, and you work. God gives, and you steward. God saves by grace, and you walk in the good works He prepared.

James isn't preaching a second gospel of earning. He's calling out a faith that nods along on Sunday and never gets up on Monday. And Paul shows us the Christian life isn't God replacing you. It's God working in you while you work.

Read these slowly. Notice who is working in each one.

bookRef.section: Traditional Christian theology does not force you to choose (middle of the Introduction)

verses.text: So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.

Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, so now, not only as in my presence but much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure.

prompts: In these verses, what does God do? What do you do?

nameIt.heading: Name it: your standstill
nameIt.body:
Now get honest. Not polished, honest. Impressive answers help no one, including you.

The Introduction names why we freeze: uncertainty hurts, failure might be public, obedience might cost comfort or money or control, and it's easier to consume inspiration than to practice faithfulness. See if one of those is yours.

Write in plain words, the way you'd say it to a friend at the kitchen table. Your journal answers are private to you.

bookRef.section: Reflection Questions, and "So why do we freeze?"

prompts: Where have I used holy language, like "I'm just trusting God" or "He'll open the door," while a clear duty was already in front of me?
In one honest sentence, what is my Great Christian Standstill right now?
What fear is under it? Uncertainty, public failure, cost, or just easier to consume than to practice?

build.heading: Build it: one clear next step
build.body:
Insight is good. Motion is better. Don't leave this stop with only a feeling.

The Introduction calls us back to a both/and: trust God as if everything depends on Him, and act as a steward of what He already put in your hand. Some of us need more rest in God's sovereignty. Some of us need more motion in stewardship. Pick the half that's thin in you right now, then write one step you can actually finish.

Keep it small. Give it a date. Name what you'll stop doing to make room. And name the one person who will ask you about it. Their job isn't to fix you. Their job is to ask.

bookRef.section: We are trying to recover a biblical both/and

prompts: Which half do I need most right now: rest in God's sovereignty, or motion in stewardship?

move.heading: Move: this week's practice
move.body:
Here's the book's practice for this week, straight from the end of the Introduction:

Name your standstill in one sentence. Tell one trusted believer. Ask them to pray with you, and to ask you next week whether you took one clear next step.

Check these off as you go. If you miss your date, don't spiral. Name what blocked you in one sentence, bring it to God, and pick a new date within three days. Grace gets you moving again. Shame freezes you all over again.
prompts: I wrote my standstill in one sentence
I told a trusted believer
I asked them to pray with me
I took one clear next step (or set a date within seven days and told them)
Missed it? New date (within three days):
move.cta: Close the app and go take your step

help.heading: Help: bring one answer, walk with one person
help.body:
Every chapter of the book ends the same way: bring one answer to a trusted believer this week. Do that first. Pick one answer you wrote here and say it out loud to someone who loves Jesus.

Then think of one person nearby who might be stuck the way you've been. You're not there to diagnose them. You may be in the same ditch. This is presence, not a rescue mission. Send one text, make one call, or ask one question and listen without fixing.

bookRef.section: Bring one answer to a trusted believer this week (closing line)

prompts: The answer I'll bring, and who I'll bring it to:

How I'll show up: one text, one call, one check-in, or one prayer
A question I could ask: "What's your standstill in one sentence?" Then listen.
help.cta: Send it, then put the phone down

pray.heading: Pray it
pray.body:
Keep it short. Pray it out loud if you can. Fill in the blanks and mean them.

Father, I stand on Your love in Jesus, not on my performance. Thank You that my acceptance was settled at the cross.

By Your Spirit, help me take this clear next step: ____.

Help me notice ____, who may be stuck the same way, and give me courage to help without pride.

Teach me the difference between holy waiting and fear wearing faith's clothes. Rest me in Your sovereignty. Move me in stewardship. In Jesus' name, amen.

review.heading: Review: after your date
review.body:
Come back after your date and tell the truth. No grades here.

Did you take the step? Is it not yet, and you can name what got in the way? Or is this a holy wait, one you can explain in a sentence, tied to what God has said in His Word, and that a trusted believer would recognize? All three are honest answers. The only answer to avoid is calling a freeze a wait.

Guardrail from the Introduction: this isn't a call to frantic busyness. Holy stillness is real. Scripture honors waiting, and the disciples waited in Jerusalem for the Spirit. We're not replacing prayer with panic. We're refusing to call a freeze faith.

The rest of the roadmap walks through each chapter of the book. If you don't have it yet, get the book to begin.
